title: am / is / are
short_description: Say who you are, how you feel and where things are — with am, is and are.
description:
Almost every English sentence needs a verb. When you describe a person, a thing or a feeling, that verb is usually am, is or are.

These three little words are the most common in the language. Learn them well and you can already build hundreds of sentences.
learning_objectives: Choose am, is or are correctly for any subject
Use the short forms (I'm, he's, they're) that native speakers use when speaking
Make negative sentences with 'm not, isn't and aren't
Use that's, there's and here's in everyday situations
Introduce yourself: your name, age, country and job

content.text:
English changes this verb depending on who you are talking about. There are only three forms to learn:

I → am
he, she, it → is
we, you, they → are

I am a student.
She is a doctor.
They are at home.
Notice that "you" always takes are — whether you mean one person or many.

In conversation, English speakers almost always join the two words together. Writing the long form is not wrong, but it can sound formal or slow.

I am → I'm
he is → he's
she is → she's
it is → it's
we are → we're
you are → you're
they are → they're

I'm from Riyadh.
He's twenty years old.
We're good friends.
Use short forms when you speak. Your English will immediately sound more natural.

To make a negative, add not after am, is or are.

I am not tired.
He is not at school.
They are not ready.

There are two ways to shorten a negative, and both are correct:

he is not → he's not  or  he isn't
we are not → we're not  or  we aren't
"I" is the exception: only I'm not is possible. There is no form "I amn't".

These three short forms appear constantly in daily conversation:

that's = that is
there's = there is
here's = here is

Thank you. That's very kind of you.
Look! There's your bus.
Here's your coffee.

With just this one verb you can already say a lot about yourself:

My name is Sara.
I'm 22.
I'm from Jeddah.
I'm a student.
My favourite colour is green.
I'm interested in music.
I'm not interested in politics.
Learn these three words well and you have the foundation of English. Everything else is built on top.

vocabulary.example: I'm tired. I want to sleep.
My brother is scared of dogs.
Steve is ill. He's in bed.

vocabulary.meaning: a person who writes news for a newspaper or TV
wanting to know more about something

exercises.prompt: Write the short form: she is
Write the short form: they are
Write the short form: it is not
Write the short form: I am not
exercises.answer: I'm not  (only this form is possible)

exercises.prompt: Complete with am, is or are: The weather ___ nice today.
Complete with am, is or are: My brother and I ___ good tennis players.
Complete with am, is or are: Emily ___ at home. Her children ___ at school.
Complete with am, is or are: I ___ a taxi driver. My sister ___ a nurse.
Complete the sentence: Steve is ill. ___ in bed.
Complete the sentence: I'm not hungry, but ___ thirsty.
Complete the sentence: Catherine isn't at home. ___ at work.
Complete the sentence: '___ your coat.' 'Oh, thank you very much.'
Now write about yourself. Answer in full sentences: What is your name? How old are you? Where are you from? What is your job? What is your favourite colour? What are you interested in?
exercises.answer: Answers will vary. Example: My name is Ali. I'm 19. I'm from Riyadh. I'm a student. My favourite colour is blue. I'm interested in football.

exercises.prompt: Write a true sentence about yourself, positive or negative: (tired)
exercises.answer: I'm tired.  or  I'm not tired.

exercises.prompt: Write a true sentence, positive or negative: (it / hot today)
exercises.answer: It's hot today.  or  It isn't hot today.
